domesticated-plants-and-animals-of-austr.name: Canoe plants
domesticated-plants-and-animals-of-austr.summary: Domesticated and semi-domesticated crops carried by Austronesian seafarers on outrigger canoes as they migrated across the Indo-Pacific from roughly 3500 to 2000 BCE.
domesticated-plants-and-animals-of-austr.source_title: Domesticated plants and animals of Austronesia

cook-islands.name: Cook Islands
cook-islands.summary: A self-governing Polynesian island nation in the South Pacific, in free association with New Zealand, made up of 15 islands with its capital at Avarua on Rarotonga.

agroforestry.name: Agroforestry
agroforestry.summary: A land-use system that integrates trees with crops or pasture for economic, environmental, and social benefits, especially practiced in the tropics.

taro.name: Taro
taro.summary: A starchy root vegetable that is a food staple across African, Caribbean, Oceanian, and East, Southeast and South Asian cultures.

marquesas-islands.name: Marquesas Islands
marquesas-islands.summary: Volcanic island group in French Polynesia, settled around the 10th century AD by voyagers from West Polynesia and named after a 16th-century Spanish viceroy of Peru.

l-au-food.name: Laulau
l-au-food.summary: One of several related Polynesian dishes made from taro leaves, often with coconut milk, meat or seafood, ranging from a soup to a dense cake.

cibotium-menziesii.name: Hāpuʻu ʻiʻi
cibotium-menziesii.summary: A tree fern species endemic to Hawaiʻi, also called the Hawaiian tree fern, whose uncoiled fronds can be eaten boiled.

austronesian-peoples.name: Austronesian peoples
austronesian-peoples.summary: Peoples descended from a prehistoric seaborne migration out of Taiwan around 3000–1500 BCE, who used sails and outrigger boats to spread across the Indo-Pacific, from Madagascar to Easter Island and New Zealand.

pulemelei-mound.name: Pulemelei Mound
pulemelei-mound.summary: The largest and oldest ancient structure in the Samoan Islands, a stone pyramid on Savai'i island built between about 1100 and 1400 AD and abandoned by 1700-1800.

savai-i.name: Savai'i
savai-i.summary: The largest and highest island in Samoa and the Samoan Islands, home to about 44,000 people, and the largest shield volcano in the South Pacific.

moai.name: Moai
moai.summary: Monolithic stone figures carved by the Rapa Nui people on Easter Island between 1250 and 1500, representing deified ancestors and set on platforms called ahu.

pohnpei.name: Pohnpei
pohnpei.summary: The largest island of the Federated States of Micronesia, home to the megalithic ruined city of Nan Madol, begun in the 8th or 9th century.

nan-madol.name: Nan Madol
nan-madol.summary: A lagoon city of artificial islets linked by canals on Pohnpei, capital of the Saudeleur dynasty until about 1628, later nicknamed the 'Venice of the Pacific.'

ali-i.name: Aliʻi
ali-i.summary: Traditional hereditary nobility of the Hawaiian islands, spanning several ranks of chiefs that could be held by men or women.

ahu-ula.name: ʻAhu ʻula
ahu-ula.summary: A feathered cape worn with a feathered helmet as a mark of the highest-ranking chiefs in ancient Hawaii; over 160 examples survive in museums worldwide.

mahiole.name: Mahiole
mahiole.summary: Traditional Hawaiian feather helmets worn with feather cloaks as symbols of the highest chiefly rank, made from woven frames decorated with bird feathers.

tongatapu.name: Tongatapu
tongatapu.summary: The main island of Tonga and site of its capital, Nukuʻalofa, home to most of the country's population and its main center of trade.

nanumea.name: Nanumea
nanumea.summary: The northwesternmost atoll of Tuvalu, a small Pacific island nation, home to about 610 people as of the 2022 census.

niutao.name: Niutao
niutao.summary: A reef island and district in the northern part of Tuvalu, with a population of about 550.

tu-i-ha-atakalaua.name: Tuʻi Haʻatakalaua
tu-i-ha-atakalaua.summary: A dynasty of Tongan monarchs founded in the 15th century that took political power from the Tuʻi Tonga line, later merging with the Tuʻi Kanokupolu dynasty by the late 18th century.

rongorongo.name: Rongorongo
rongorongo.summary: A system of glyphs found on Easter Island, discovered in the 19th century, that resembles writing but has never been deciphered; if genuine, it would be a rare independent invention of writing.

oro.name: ʻOro
oro.summary: A god of war worshipped mainly in Tahiti and the Society Islands during the 17th and 18th centuries, closely linked to the secret Arioi society.

tangata-manu.name: Tangata manu
tangata-manu.summary: Winner of a traditional Rapa Nui (Easter Island) competition to retrieve the season's first sooty tern egg from the islet of Motu Nui and climb the cliffs to Orongo.

reimiro.name: Reimiro
reimiro.summary: A crescent-shaped wooden pectoral ornament worn by Easter Islanders, carved with a human face on each end and representing a Polynesian canoe.

boustrophedon.name: Boustrophedon
boustrophedon.summary: A writing style in which alternate lines run in reverse, mirror-image directions, common on ancient Greek inscriptions and other early scripts.

hotu-matu-a.name: Hotu Matu'a
hotu-matu-a.summary: Legendary first settler and supreme chief of Easter Island, said to have arrived by canoe with colonists from the Polynesian homeland of Hiva and founded the clans of the Rapa Nui people.

society-islands.name: Society Islands
society-islands.summary: An archipelago in Polynesia in the South Pacific, part of French Polynesia, whose largest island is Tahiti; settlers from here later helped populate other Pacific islands.

tuvalu.name: Tuvalu
tuvalu.summary: A small Polynesian island country in the Pacific, first settled by Polynesians migrating from Samoa and Tonga around three thousand years ago.

tu-i-tonga.name: Tuʻi Tonga
tu-i-tonga.summary: A line of Tongan kings beginning in the 10th century with the mythical ʻAhoʻeitu, holding political power until yielding to the Tuʻi Haʻatakalaua in the 15th century; the title itself ended in 1865.

tu-i-kanokupolu.name: Tuʻi Kanokupolu
tu-i-kanokupolu.summary: A junior royal rank within Tonga's king's lineage, created to share regional rule, whose holders grew increasingly dominant over Tonga.

pa-ao.name: Paʻao
pa-ao.summary: A figure in Hawaiian tradition, a high priest said to have arrived from Samoa and introduced customs such as human sacrifice and worship of the god Kū, installing a new chief in place of Kapawā.

kahuna.name: Kahuna
kahuna.summary: Hawaiian word for an expert in any field, historically used for priests, doctors, ministers and sorcerers.

upolu.name: Upolu
upolu.summary: The most populous island of Samoa, home to the capital Apia, formed by a basaltic shield volcano and described as the first woman in Samoan mythology.

kamehameha-i.name: Kamehameha I
kamehameha-i.summary: Conqueror and first ruler of the Kingdom of Hawaii, known as Kamehameha the Great, honored with a statue in the U.S. National Statuary Hall Collection.

s-lote-tupou-iii.name: Queen Sālote
s-lote-tupou-iii.summary: Queen of Tonga from 1918 until her death in 1965, reigning nearly 48 years, the longest of any Tongan monarch, in a period seen as a golden age for Tonga.

k-ne.name: Kāne
k-ne.summary: The highest of the three major Hawaiian deities, worshipped as the god of procreation, creator of life, and ancestor of chiefs and commoners, associated with dawn, sun and sky.

k.name: Kū
k.summary: One of the four great gods of Hawaiian religion, worshiped under many names including Kūkāʻilimoku, whose rites uniquely included human sacrifice.

lono.name: Lono
lono.summary: A Hawaiian god of fertility, agriculture, rain, music and peace, honored during the annual Makahiki festival.

kanaloa.name: Kanaloa
kanaloa.summary: A Hawaiian god symbolized by the squid or octopus, associated with the ocean and seamanship, and traditionally paired with the god Kāne.

tapu-polynesian-culture.name: Tapu
tapu-polynesian-culture.summary: A Polynesian concept of something holy or sacred involving rules and prohibitions; the source of the English word "taboo", from Captain Cook's 1777 visit to Tonga.

marae.name: Marae
marae.summary: A communal or sacred cleared ground used for religious and social purposes in Polynesian societies, still vital in some cultures today though abandoned in others after Christianity arrived.

rano-raraku.name: Rano Raraku
rano-raraku.summary: Volcanic crater on Easter Island that served as a quarry for about 500 years, supplying the stone for roughly 95% of the island's moai statues.

polynesian-triangle.name: Polynesian Triangle
polynesian-triangle.summary: The vast Pacific Ocean region defined by Hawaii, Easter Island and New Zealand at its three corners, commonly used to mark the extent of Polynesia.

vanua.name: vanua
vanua.summary: An Austronesian word, from Fijian and Melanesian languages, meaning 'land', 'home' or 'village', used for small settlements.

kapu-hawaiian-culture.name: Kapu
kapu-hawaiian-culture.summary: The ancient Hawaiian code of laws governing lifestyle, gender roles, politics, and religion, in which breaking a rule was often punished by death; related to the Polynesian concept of taboo.

arauco-peninsula.name: Arauco Peninsula
arauco-peninsula.summary: A peninsula in southern Chile projecting northwest into the Pacific Ocean, west of the Cordillera de Nahuelbuta.

christopher-columbus.name: Christopher Columbus
christopher-columbus.summary: Italian explorer and navigator (1451–1506) whose four Spanish-sponsored voyages opened the way for European exploration and colonization of the Americas.
